I'm 28 years old, going back to college, first class is Math. I'm contemplating shooting myself.

I'm your age. Let me tell you a story.

I went to college for the first time when I was 18 and graduated with a degree I hated, not the degree I came for, and then went and pissed away a few years. Then my bride (got married after college) told me that if I never went back for that other degree, I'd regret it. I have a father who never finished his associates and he talks to me with a venomous jealousy. So I went back. I was taking classes with kids I mentored as a senior and alumni. I was getting a very specific five-year communications degree which culminates in a senior address and I shared the stage with these kids.

But in the process, I reconnected with a man named Ernie. Let me tell you about Ernie.

Ernie was fat. Ernie was a father. Ernie lived in a house two-hours from campus. Ernie was below the average IQ in the dorm.

Ernie was also the kindest man I met there. He was Fifty-Two and going back to college — his daughter was almost ready for college. He and a guy named Adam — also a non-trad aged around 39 — lived in the same dorm room Tuesday through Thursday nights and then would drive home on Friday morning. On Thursday nights, they even stayed with us kids when we had this dorm community night thing where people would come and give inspiring speeches and we'd share drinks and shitty food and make stupid jokes. Culture creation stuff, you know how dorms are.

Can I tell you that we had three valedictorians go through that dorm in five years and all of them said that Ernie and Adam made them want to learn?

When I reconnected with Ernie during my second degree, he said, "When I went to school for the first time, I went because I was told to and I kind of, sort of wanted to. When came back to school as an old man, I came back because I needed it. I need to learn like I need water."

And I spent that year — the year of my second bachelor degree — learning more than in my other four years combined. I learned stuff outside of classes. I came up with creative ways to fulfill assignments in lame classes so that they aligned. Hell, I had one professor that let me fulfill the semester project by self-publishing a book. The academic dean, by the end of it, let me create a class :: DO 505 — Mythology and Modern Fiction. I was the only student and he was the only teacher. And it was beautiful.

Did I graduate cum laude? Hell no.

Did I graduate as some class star? Well of course not, I didn't know hardly anyone in my class.

But I learned more in that year than in the other four combined and it was because I needed to learn. I needed to learn how to learn. How to become an autodidact.

Ernie taught me that.

Hope it helps. Hang in there — even the dumbest most meaningless classes can hold surprises if you look for them.
